story.title: Huawei Found Guilty of Conspiracy to Steal Trade Secrets and Bank Fraud
story.summary: A U.S. jury has convicted Huawei Technologies of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud. The company was accused of stealing technology from U.S. firms, violating U.S. sanctions by doing business with countries like Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to government officials and banks. This conviction represents a significant legal challenge for the Chinese tech giant.

explore_lenses.label: Why does the split verdict matter?
explore_lenses.title: Most charges stood, but the broadest theory failed
explore_lenses.summary: The jury convicted Huawei and three subsidiaries on 10 counts, while rejecting the government's racketeering and obstruction-conspiracy counts. That preserves major criminal findings but limits the government's argument that Huawei itself was a unified criminal enterprise.

claims.text: The Justice Department said the guilty verdicts covered trade-secret conspiracy, bank and wire fraud, Iran-related sanctions violations, conspiracy to defraud the United States, and money-laundering conspiracy.
The jury acquitted Huawei of racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice, according to contemporaneous court reporting.

Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig characterized the racketeering acquittal as a rejection of the government's overarching narrative; prosecutors had argued that theft, sanctions evasion and bank deception were coordinated corporate conduct.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The practical commercial effect outside the United States is not yet clear; reporting notes that Huawei has already been excluded from U.S. carrier equipment sales for years.

explore_lenses.label: How did Huawei's case reach a jury?
explore_lenses.title: A long-running case combined IP and Iran allegations
explore_lenses.summary: The prosecution grew from separate 2019 trade-secret and financial-fraud cases into a wider 2020 indictment. It reached trial after years of litigation and delays, with the government alleging a long-running pattern rather than a single episode.

claims.text: In January 2019, a federal grand jury in Washington charged Huawei entities with conspiracy and attempted theft of T-Mobile trade secrets, wire fraud, and obstruction-related conduct.
A February 2020 superseding indictment in Brooklyn added racketeering and trade-secret-conspiracy allegations and alleged concealed activity involving Iran and North Korea.

In 2021, then-Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou entered a deferred-prosecution agreement and admitted misleading a global financial institution about Huawei's relationship with Skycom and its Iran business; that was a separate resolution from the corporate case.
Huawei's defense argued at trial that prosecutors turned isolated misconduct by some employees into an unsupported claim of company-wide criminality.

explore_lenses.label: What happens before the case is final?
explore_lenses.title: Sentencing is set, and Huawei says it will appeal
explore_lenses.summary: The trial court must impose sentence before the appellate process is complete. Huawei has said it will challenge the convictions, while prosecutors can seek monetary consequences against the company and its subsidiaries.

claims.text: The Justice Department states that sentencing is set for September 14, 2027, and that the judge will consider the Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.
The Justice Department says the corporate defendants face possible criminal fines, forfeiture and restitution at sentencing.
Federal law allows an organization to be fined up to the greatest applicable amount, including twice the gross gain from an offense or twice the victims' gross loss when that alternative is used.
Huawei attorney Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal the convictions; Huawei separately said it would take legal action to defend its rights and interests.

story_report.summary: A U.S. jury found Huawei guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank and wire fraud, Iran-related sanctions violations, conspiracy to defraud the United States and money-laundering conspiracy. The verdict leaves the Chinese technology company facing sentencing, with possible criminal fines, forfeiture and restitution. Huawei has said it will challenge the convictions, while the eventual penalty and the outcome of any appeal remain unresolved.

sections.heading: Huawei Case Spanned Years of Charges
sections.body: Federal prosecutors first charged Huawei entities in Washington in January 2019 with conspiracy and attempted theft of T-Mobile trade secrets, wire fraud and obstruction-related conduct. A 2020 superseding indictment in Brooklyn added racketeering and trade-secret-conspiracy allegations and alleged concealed activity involving Iran and North Korea. Separately, former Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou entered a deferred-prosecution agreement in 2021 concerning statements about Huawei’s relationship with Skycom and its Iran business.

sections.heading: Huawei Defense Contested Corporate Liability
sections.body: The jury acquitted Huawei of racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice, according to court reporting. Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig said the racketeering acquittal rejected the government’s broader narrative of coordinated corporate misconduct. At trial, the defense argued that prosecutors had improperly portrayed isolated employee conduct as company-wide criminality.

sections.heading: Huawei Sentencing and Appeal Remain Ahead
sections.body: The Justice Department says sentencing is scheduled for Sept. 14, 2027, when the judge will consider the Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. The corporate defendants could face fines, forfeiture and restitution; federal law can permit an organizational fine based on twice an offense’s gross gain or victims’ gross loss. Heberlig said Huawei would appeal, and the company said it would take legal action to defend its rights and interests.

unresolved.text: The size of any fine, forfeiture or restitution award, whether Huawei secures a stay, and the timing and outcome of an appeal have not been determined.
The commercial effect of the verdict outside the United States remains unclear; reporting notes Huawei has already been excluded from U.S. carrier-equipment sales for years.

related_stories.title: Huawei Convicted of Trade Secrets Theft, Acquitted of Racketeering Charges
related_stories.summary: A federal jury in Brooklyn found Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts related to stealing trade secrets and deceiving banks about its business in Iran. However, the company was acquitted of the more serious charge of engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. The verdict concludes a months-long trial.

related_stories.title: China Reveals Crew for Upcoming Space Mission Including Pakistani Astronaut
related_stories.summary: China has announced the crew for its upcoming Shenzhou-24 mission, which includes Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a Pakistani astronaut. Ali will be the first foreigner to board China's Tiangong space station. The mission is set to launch on Wednesday.
